label: Must Be True
oneLiner: Treat the stimulus as proven facts; the answer must follow from them with certainty.
definition: Must Be True questions ask what is guaranteed by the stimulus. The stimulus is usually a fact set, not an argument. The correct answer is often a combination of two statements, a contrapositive, or a modest paraphrase—never something merely likely.
objectives: Combine statements (especially conditionals and quantifiers) to derive guaranteed inferences
Reject answers that are merely probable or that add information

examples.text: If every bakery on the street closes at 6 and Mira’s is a bakery on the street, Mira’s closes at 6.
If every statute requires publication to take effect and the act was never published, it has not taken effect.
If all A-rated bonds in a fund are euro-denominated and most holdings are A-rated, most holdings are euro-denominated.

attack: Identify the type: the stimulus is evidence, the answer is proven
Translate conditionals and quantifiers into arrows
Combine statements; look for chains and contrapositives
Prove each answer: can you point to the lines that guarantee it?
Eliminate anything that could be false
correctLooksLike: An answer you can prove line-by-line from the stimulus—often modest, often a chain or contrapositive.
traps: Too Strong: “always”, “most” when only “some” is supported
Out of Scope: true in life, not in the stimulus
commonError: Choosing an answer that is very likely true in the real world but not guaranteed by the stimulus.

keyPoints.point: The stimulus is accepted as true
The correct answer must be proven, not just likely
Look for combinations, chains, and contrapositives

card.front: In a Must Be True question, how certain must the correct answer be?
card.back: 100% certain—it must follow from the stimulus with no added assumptions.

label: Most Strongly Supported
oneLiner: The answer need not be certain—but it must be the claim the stimulus supports best.
definition: MSS questions relax the certainty standard slightly: the correct answer is the one the facts most strongly support, typically a modest, hedged claim (“can”, “some”, “may”). Wrong answers either overreach or drift out of scope.
objectives: Distinguish strong support from certainty
Prefer modest answers tightly tied to specific lines

examples.text: A friend arrives soaked and holding a closed umbrella: it most likely rained, though not certainly.
Courts that permit dissents have longer opinions; this supports that permitting dissents can influence length.
Yields rose each time a central bank paired a hold with inflation forecasts: investor reactions can depend on accompanying information.

attack: Read the facts carefully; note qualifiers (usually, some, most)
Predict a modest conclusion the facts point toward
Prefer answers with hedges matching the evidence
Eliminate over-strong and out-of-scope answers
correctLooksLike: A cautious claim (“can”, “some”, “may”) backed by a specific sentence.
traps: Shell Game swaps of the measured quantity
commonError: Picking a bold, interesting conclusion over a modest, well-supported one.

keyPoints.point: Tie the answer to specific lines

card.back: MSS requires strong support rather than certainty; modest, hedged answers tied to the facts usually win.

label: Cannot Be True
oneLiner: Find the answer that contradicts what the stimulus proves.
definition: Cannot Be True (and “could be true EXCEPT”) questions ask for the one answer inconsistent with the stimulus. Four answers could be true (or must be true); the correct answer is impossible given the facts.
objectives: Derive what must be true, then find its contradiction
Recognize the “EXCEPT” variants

examples.text: If the store is closed every Sunday, “I bought bread there last Sunday” cannot be true.
If an unsigned bill became law only via a two-thirds re-passage that the Senate reserves for budget bills, “it was not a budget bill” cannot be true.
If most disclosing funds are audited and audited funds never default, “most disclosing funds defaulted” cannot be true.

attack: Derive the guaranteed inferences first
Look for an answer that contradicts one of them
Answers that could be true are wrong—even if surprising
Double-check EXCEPT wording
correctLooksLike: A statement that directly contradicts a premise or a derived inference.
traps: Answers that are merely unsupported (could still be true)
commonError: Selecting an answer that is unsupported—which is still possible, and therefore not the answer.

keyPoints.point: Unsupported is not the same as impossible

card.front: In Cannot Be True, why is an unsupported answer wrong?
card.back: Unsupported claims could still be true; the right answer must be impossible given the stimulus.

label: Main Conclusion
oneLiner: Identify the claim everything else supports.
definition: Main Conclusion questions ask you to identify (or paraphrase) the argument’s overall conclusion. Traps include sub-conclusions, premises, and the opposing view the author rejects.
objectives: Locate the main conclusion anywhere in a stimulus
Distinguish it from sub-conclusions and counterpoints

examples.text: “Skip the 8:15 train—it’s always late, and the 8:30 gets you there first.” Conclusion: skip the 8:15.
“The critics’ fear is misplaced, since the treaty bars political extraditions.” Conclusion: the fear is misplaced.
“The recommendation should be rejected; reported returns understate volatility.” Conclusion: reject.

attack: Find candidate conclusions (claims the author argues for)
Apply the Why? test between candidates
If X supports Y, Y is higher in the structure
Paraphrase; match the answer to your paraphrase
correctLooksLike: A faithful paraphrase of the claim that every other statement ultimately supports.
commonError: Choosing the sub-conclusion that follows “so” instead of the claim it supports.

keyPoints.point: Every premise ultimately supports the main conclusion

card.front: How do you tell a main conclusion from a sub-conclusion?
card.back: The sub-conclusion supports the main conclusion; apply the Why? test—the main conclusion is supported but supports nothing further.

label: Role of a Statement
chapter: CHAPTER III — ROLE OF A STATEMENT
oneLiner: Describe what job a particular claim does in the argument.
definition: Role questions name a statement and ask its function: main conclusion, premise, sub-conclusion, counterpoint, concession, or evidence against a view the author rejects. Answers are abstract, so match the role, not the content.
objectives: Assign a role to any quoted statement
Read abstract role descriptions precisely

examples.text: “It’s true the gym is pricey, but the classes are worth it” — “pricey” is a concession.
“Opponents argue judges are unelected” — the opponents’ premise the author rebuts.
“Pigments were sold to dozens of workshops” — undermines evidence for a view the author rejects.

attack: Diagram the argument first
Locate the referenced statement
Ask: is it supported? does it support? whose view is it?
Match each clause of the answer to the diagram
correctLooksLike: An abstract description where every clause matches your diagram.
traps: Answers that describe the right claim with the wrong function
commonError: Reading only the first half of a two-part role answer.

keyPoints.point: Check every clause of the answer

stemCues: plays which one of the following roles

card.front: A statement is supported by premises and also supports the main conclusion. Its role?

label: Method of Reasoning
oneLiner: Describe HOW the argument argues, in abstract terms.
definition: Method questions ask you to describe an argument’s technique: analogy, counterexample, alternative explanation, reductio, appeal to principle, attacking evidence. Answers are abstract; test each phrase against the stimulus.
objectives: Name common argumentative techniques
Translate a stimulus into abstract description

examples.text: “By your logic, we should also ban cars” — refutation by analogy.
“The firm blames the competitor, but sales fell where it hasn’t entered” — undermining an explanation.
“That reading makes the clause contradict itself” — reductio ad absurdum.

attack: Diagram the argument
Describe its method in your own abstract words
Test each answer phrase by phrase
Eliminate answers that describe something that did not happen
correctLooksLike: An abstract description you can map onto each move in the stimulus.
traps: Answers describing a flaw the argument did not commit
commonError: Accepting an answer because one phrase fits while another describes something absent.

keyPoints.point: Common methods: analogy, counterexample, alternative explanation

card.front: “By that reasoning, the medical exam should be abolished too.” Method?
card.back: Refutation by analogy: same reasoning yields an unacceptable conclusion.

label: Flaw
oneLiner: Name the error that makes the conclusion fail to follow.
definition: Flaw questions ask what is wrong with the reasoning. The premises are accepted as true; the error lies in the leap to the conclusion. Most flaws come from a recurring library of fifteen patterns.
objectives: Diagnose the gap between premises and conclusion
Match it to the flaw library
Read abstract answer language precisely

examples.text: “Every time I wash my car it rains—washing causes rain.” Causation from correlation.
“The bill must be unconstitutional: its sponsor has been indicted.” Ad hominem.
“82% of an arbitration journal’s readers prefer arbitration, so most businesses do.” Biased sample.

attack: Find the conclusion and premises
Locate the gap: what is assumed?
Name the flaw in plain words
Match to an abstract answer
Reject answers that attack premises or describe absent errors
correctLooksLike: An abstract description of the specific leap the argument makes, e.g. “overlooks an alternative cause.”
traps: Answers attacking a premise (premises are given)
Real flaws that this argument did not commit
commonError: Picking a description of a flaw that sounds familiar but does not occur in this stimulus.

keyPoints.point: Premises are accepted; the leap is the problem

card.front: In a Flaw question, can the correct answer say a premise is false?
card.back: No. Premises are accepted; the flaw is in the reasoning from premises to conclusion.

label: Necessary Assumption
oneLiner: Find the claim the argument cannot do without; negate it and the argument collapses.
definition: A necessary assumption is a statement that must be true for the argument to work. It need not make the conclusion certain. The Negation Test identifies it: negate the answer; if the argument falls apart, it was necessary.
objectives: Apply the Negation Test fluently
Distinguish necessary from sufficient
Spot defender assumptions that rule out alternatives

examples.text: “I’ll drive to Vienna tonight”—assumes the car has fuel (or can get it).
“The citations show advisory opinions have effect”—assumes the opinions influenced at least some decisions.
“The switch to index funds improved returns”—assumes the market rise alone does not explain it.

attack: Find conclusion and premises; locate the gap
Predict: what must be true for this to work?
Negate each contender
Prefer weaker, minimal statements
Check that the answer is relevant to the gap
correctLooksLike: A minimal claim whose negation destroys the argument—often “not all”, “at least some”, or “does not entirely”.
traps: Too Strong: sufficient but not necessary
Strengtheners that are helpful but not required
commonError: Choosing a strong answer that would prove the conclusion but is not required by it.

card.front: How does the Negation Test work?
card.back: Negate the answer choice; if the argument falls apart, the answer is a necessary assumption.

label: Sufficient Assumption
oneLiner: Add the premise that makes the conclusion guaranteed.
definition: A sufficient assumption, added to the premises, makes the conclusion follow with certainty. These answers are often strong and conditional: they bridge the rogue term in the premises to the rogue term in the conclusion.
objectives: Identify rogue terms in premise and conclusion
Build the bridge conditional
Recognize that strong answers are welcome here

examples.text: “It’s Monday, so the museum is closed”—sufficient: the museum is closed every Monday.
“Signed during an illegal blockade, so voidable”—bridge: blockade → duress (duress → voidable given).
“Reserves fall short, so Tavria will devalue”—bridge: peg fails → devaluation.

attack: Diagram premises and conclusion as arrows
Find the term in the conclusion missing from the premises
Bridge: (premise term) → (conclusion term)
Check direction; reversals fail
Prove the conclusion with the answer added
correctLooksLike: A (usually conditional) statement that, with the premises, deductively proves the conclusion.
commonError: Choosing a reversed conditional because it mentions the right terms.
stemCues: allows the conclusion to be properly inferred

card.front: SA vs. NA in one line?
card.back: SA: enough to guarantee the conclusion (can be strong). NA: required for the argument (often minimal).

label: Strengthen
oneLiner: Add information that makes the conclusion more likely.
definition: Strengthen answers may introduce new information (“if true”). They help by closing the gap: ruling out alternatives, confirming a mechanism, or showing the cause-effect pattern holds.
objectives: Strengthen causal, sampling, and analogy arguments
Prefer answers that target the gap

examples.text: “The plant caused the frog decline” + “nitrate levels rose to harmful levels after it opened.”
“The commission made the guarantees last” + “violations rose after it was dissolved.”
“Buybacks correct undervaluation” + “buybacks by overvalued firms produce no rise despite confident signals.”

attack: Find the conclusion and the gap
Predict: what would make the leap safer?
Accept new information
Pick the answer that hits the gap hardest
correctLooksLike: New information that closes or narrows the gap—often eliminating an alternative or confirming the mechanism.
commonError: Choosing an answer that repeats a premise rather than adding new support.

card.front: Three classic ways to strengthen a causal argument?
card.back: Rule out alternative causes; show cause present → effect present; show cause absent → effect absent (or confirm the mechanism).

label: Weaken
oneLiner: Add information that makes the conclusion less likely.
definition: Weaken answers attack the gap between premises and conclusion: alternative causes, unrepresentative samples, broken mechanisms, or disanalogies. They need not disprove the conclusion.
objectives: Identify the vulnerability before reading answers
Prefer broad attacks on the mechanism over marginal dents

examples.text: “My new diet worked—I lost 5 kg” + “you also started running daily.”
“Class actions cause compliance” + “those countries also have well-funded regulators.”
“Tax cut will boost investment” + “most firms report losses and pay no tax.”

attack: Find conclusion and gap
Predict the strongest attack
Accept new information
Choose the answer that most damages the link
correctLooksLike: New information that opens the gap: an alternative cause, a biased sample, or a failed mechanism.
commonError: Picking an answer that weakens “some” cases over one that breaks the mechanism broadly.

keyPoints.point: Attack the gap, not the premises

card.front: Must a weakener prove the conclusion false?
card.back: No—it only needs to make the conclusion less likely.

label: Evaluate
oneLiner: Find the question whose answer would strengthen or weaken the argument.
definition: Evaluate questions ask what would be most useful to know. Use the Variance Test: answer the question both ways; if one answer strengthens and the other weakens, it is relevant.
objectives: Run the Variance Test
Recognize alternative-cause and pre-existing-trend questions

examples.text: “Did the cranes cause faster docking?”—ask whether ship sizes changed.
“Did PR sustain turnout?”—ask whether the trend predated the reform.
“Is the fund manager skilled?”—ask whether outperformance came from extra risk.

attack: Find the gap
For each answer, imagine “yes” and “no”
Keep answers where yes/no push the argument in opposite directions
Pick the one aimed at the gap
correctLooksLike: A question targeting the argument’s key assumption—often an alternative explanation.
traps: Questions whose answers don’t matter either way
commonError: Choosing a question that is interesting but whose answer wouldn’t change your view of the argument.

keyPoints.point: Relevant answers flip the argument’s strength

card.back: Answer the proposed question both ways; if the two answers strengthen and weaken respectively, it is relevant to evaluating the argument.

label: Parallel Reasoning
oneLiner: Match the logical form of the argument, regardless of subject.
definition: Parallel questions ask which answer has the same reasoning pattern. Abstract the stimulus into its form (conditional chain, quantifier pattern, rule-exception) and match strength of language and direction.
objectives: Abstract a stimulus into symbols
Match conclusion type and strength first

examples.text: “All cats purr; Tom is a cat; Tom purrs” parallels “All judges are lawyers; Ana is a judge; Ana is a lawyer.”
“Most judges were arbitrators; all arbitrators favor the rules” ↔ “Most paintings are Flemish; all Flemish paintings were restored.”
A rule–exception–rule displaced pattern appears in contract excuse and exam exemptions alike.

attack: Abstract the stimulus (A → B → C; A; ∴ C)
Check conclusion type (certain, probable, recommendation)
Eliminate mismatched conclusions quickly
Compare the remaining answers’ forms
correctLooksLike: An argument with the same form, quantifier strength, and conclusion type—in a different subject.
commonError: Matching subject matter or word order instead of logical form.

card.front: First filter on a Parallel question?
card.back: Match the conclusion type and strength (certain/probable/recommendation; all/most/some).

label: Parallel Flaw
oneLiner: Find the answer that makes the same mistake.
definition: Parallel Flaw combines Flaw and Parallel: name the stimulus’s error, then find an answer committing the identical error. Valid arguments and different flaws are wrong.
objectives: Name the flaw before reading answers
Distinguish sibling flaws (reversal vs. negation; part→whole vs. whole→part)

examples.text: “Each chapter is concise, so the book is concise” ↔ “each clause is easy, so the treaty is easy.”
“Ratified → binding; binding; so ratified” ↔ “released → aged; aged; so released.”
“The merger may be blocked; if blocked, shares fall; so they will fall” ↔ “strike may happen; strike → negotiation; so negotiation.”

attack: Name the flaw
Eliminate valid answers
Eliminate answers with a different flaw
Confirm direction and modality match
correctLooksLike: An answer with the same error in the same direction—e.g., reversal, not negation.
commonError: Picking an answer with a related but different flaw (negation instead of reversal).

card.back: Negation (denying the sufficient)—not the same as Reversal (B; so A).

label: Principle — Identify
oneLiner: Find the general rule that justifies the argument or judgment.
definition: Principle–Identify questions are general-form Sufficient Assumption or Strengthen questions: the principle’s trigger must match the facts, and its outcome must match the conclusion.
objectives: Match trigger to facts and outcome to conclusion
Handle “even if” and priority judgments

examples.text: “You shouldn’t have read my diary—it was private” ← “It is wrong to read private writings without consent.”
Upland was wrong to endanger uninvolved residents ← “Disputes must not endanger non-parties.”
Board acted improperly despite reasonable pay ← “Reliance on beneficiary-chosen advisers is improper regardless of outcome.”

attack: Identify the judgment and its stated reason
Predict: if [reason], then [judgment]
Check each answer’s trigger and outcome
Watch “even if” clauses
correctLooksLike: A general conditional whose trigger fits the stated reasons and whose result is the stated conclusion.
traps: Principles leading to the opposite outcome
commonError: Choosing a principle that sounds noble but would not produce the argument’s conclusion.

card.front: Principle–Identify is most like which other type?
card.back: Sufficient Assumption (in general form)—the principle bridges reasons to judgment.

label: Principle — Apply
oneLiner: Apply a stated rule to find the judgment it supports.
definition: Principle–Apply gives you the rule and asks which case conforms to it. Translate the principle into conditionals; check each answer’s facts against the trigger and its judgment against the outcome. “Only if” principles can condemn but never certify.
objectives: Translate principles into conditionals
Avoid using necessary conditions to certify

examples.text: Rule: “Late arrivals may not enter until intermission.” Case: Jo arrived late and waited—conforms.
Rule: arbitrator withdraws on reasonable doubt unless all parties consent; both consented → need not withdraw.
Rule: commission products only if disclosed and suitable; undisclosed → improper.

attack: Translate the principle (trigger → outcome; exceptions)
For each answer: is the trigger met?
Does the judgment match what the rule requires?
Beware certifying with necessary conditions
correctLooksLike: A case whose facts satisfy the rule and whose judgment is exactly what the rule implies.
commonError: Concluding something is permitted because it meets a rule’s necessary conditions.
stemCues: conforms most closely to the principle
most clearly justified by the principle

card.front: A rule says “X may do Y only if A and B.” X meets A and B. Is Y permitted?
card.back: Not established—A and B are necessary, not sufficient. The rule can only condemn failures.

label: Resolve the Paradox
oneLiner: Explain how two apparently conflicting facts can both be true.
definition: Paradox questions present facts in tension. The correct answer introduces a factor that allows both to be true—typically a second mechanism, a difference between groups, or a change in conditions.
objectives: State the tension in one sentence
Find answers that explain both facts

examples.text: A restaurant is always empty yet thriving: most revenue comes from catering.
Policy rate cut but mortgage rates rose: long-term yields rose on inflation expectations.
More taxis but fares unchanged: operating costs doubled.

attack: State the paradox (“X, yet Y”)
Predict factors that would make both true
Eliminate answers that explain only one side or deepen the puzzle
Choose the answer that reconciles both
correctLooksLike: A new fact that makes both sides of the tension expected.
commonError: Choosing an answer that explains why one fact happened while ignoring the other.

card.front: What must a paradox resolution do?
card.back: Allow BOTH facts to be true—usually by adding a factor that explains the unexpected one.

label: Point at Issue
oneLiner: Find the claim on which two speakers hold opposite views.
definition: Point at Issue questions show a dialogue. The correct answer is a claim on which both speakers express opinions—and the opinions conflict. Use the agree/disagree test for each speaker.
objectives: Run the two-speaker test
Recognize disputes about weight rather than facts

examples.text: Ana: “The film was too long.” Ben: “Every minute was necessary.” Issue: whether the film was too long.
Katalin: no damages; Andrei: entitled to compensation. Issue: whether damages were owed.
Mira: volatility disqualifies equities; Tomás: decade value matters more. Issue: whether volatility is decisive.

attack: Summarize each speaker’s conclusion
For each answer: Speaker 1? Speaker 2?
Keep only answers with opposing opinions from both
Prefer the conclusions as the clash
correctLooksLike: A claim both speakers address, with opposite positions.
commonError: Choosing a claim one speaker makes and the other simply ignores.

card.front: Two conditions for a Point at Issue answer?
card.back: Both speakers express an opinion on it, and their opinions conflict.

label: Point of Agreement
oneLiner: Find the claim both speakers are committed to.
definition: Point of Agreement questions ask what both speakers accept. Agreement often lives in concessions or shared premises, even when their conclusions differ.
objectives: Find shared premises and concessions
Avoid claims only one speaker makes

examples.text: Two friends argue about the restaurant’s value but agree the food was cold.
Eszter and Lorant both reject the court’s quick-entry rationale.
Hannah and Viktor both accept that compliance is costly for small issuers.

attack: Summarize each speaker
Highlight concessions (“admittedly”, “true”, “indeed”)
Test each answer against both speakers
Pick the claim both commit to
correctLooksLike: A claim that appears (or is clearly implied) in both speeches.
commonError: Picking a conclusion one speaker states and assuming the other agrees.
stemCues: most strongly supports that they agree

card.front: Where does agreement usually hide in a dialogue?
card.back: In concessions and shared premises, not in the conclusions.
